#10621. Goldman Sachs bans non-engineers from using advanced AI tools

Goldman Sachs has banned traders, bankers, and other staff from using advanced AI coding tools because of risk and productivity concerns.

The bank is limiting access to tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub to engineers and so-called “strats”—an investment banking term for workers who specialize in quantitative engineering and analytics—Bloomberg reported this week.

The move reportedly frustrated traders who used the tools to monitor data, build financial models, and produce graphics, among other things.

It also appears to undermine comments from Goldman chief information officer Marco Argenti in July, when he praised nontechnical staff using AI to build software prototypes before passing them to engineers for refinement.

A Goldman spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company allows staff to experiment with certain AI tools “to determine the best use cases across different parts of the firm” and to assess “a variety of factors including productivity and risk management.”

Once the experimental period ends, “we put [the tools] in the hands of those who are best suited to leverage them for the long term,” he said. 

Fast Company reached out to Goldman Sachs for additional comment but had not heard back by the time of publication. 

Wall Street institutions have been wrestling with how to balance speed versus safety in AI adoption. Last month, JPMorgan Chase chief information officer Lori Beer said that artificial intelligence is evolving so quickly that it can be difficult to assess the risks in real time.

“We want to move at speed, but sometimes we must pull back to get controls in place,” she said. “The technology is running ahead of capabilities to manage it.”

Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan has urged caution about allowing AI agents to operate without human supervision, specifically saying investment bankers need to carefully check the accuracy of AI-generated pitchbooks and spreadsheets. “The risk [is] letting it start getting answers without humans checking to make sure the answer was right,” he said in September.

Of course, banks also remain eager to capitalize on AI’s potential benefits.  

Goldman’s internal AI initiatives include a proprietary chatbot, which is available to all employees, and a “copilot” coding tool for developers. As of September 2025, it was also piloting an autonomous coding agent and a copilot tool for investment bankers to help them compile research.

#10617. Anthropic’s AI development has doubled in speed despite slowdown calls, research group says

Anthropic is developing its artificial intelligence systems around twice as quickly as it was a year ago amid the CEO’s calls to slow down the technology’s pace of improvement, according to an analysis released Thursday by an independent monitoring group.

Anthropic invited researchers from the Berkeley, California-based nonprofit, Model Evaluation and Threat Research, to review its internal data and interview staff as it prepares for its Wall Street debut with debate swirling over the potential for AI models to elude human control with catastrophic consequences.

The findings are significant because details about the technology—and its risks—have been provided primarily by AI companies, which have been encouraged by President Donald Trump’s administration to police themselves on matters of safety.

It was during the research group’s assessment period that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow its work so safety measures can catch up. In a Sept. 12 essay responding to mounting concerns about runaway AI, he urged the AI world to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

Anthropic did not immediately comment on the report in response to inquiries.

The San Francisco-based company is planning to go public later this month in what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever.

AI is playing a bigger role in its own improvement

METR estimated that Anthropic is improving the capabilities of its models to do “well specified tasks” around twice as fast as it was a year earlier. The nonprofit’s researchers said they believed much of the reason for the faster development is the help of AI itself.

Anthropic has said its Claude chatbot is increasingly helping the company develop newer, more advanced versions of itself.

METR has conducted evaluations on model capabilities for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other labs for years. The nonprofit is funded through donations and does not accept compensation for its work, but AI companies it has partnered with for evaluations have provided access and tokens, which METR uses for evaluations, research and engineering.

One of its two reports was based on analysis of Anthropic’s internal data provided by the company over a period of about 11 weeks, from mid-August through late October, as well as employee interviews.

METR said its assessment focused on two questions: whether the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities has accelerated and how much of that was attributable to AI. The group said it was given “unprecedented access to internal data” on Anthropic’s AI research and development process.

Anthropic’s redactions to the report limited how METR could communicate more detailed estimates of acceleration, and there were some internal disagreements and uncertainty among METR’s team, but the group said it believed the company’s rate of improvement had doubled.

“Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025,” according to the METR report.

METR also reviewed both a public risk report Anthropic published in August and a private version, as well as other non-public data, and the organization said the public report “overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring.”

Assessors see little holding back AI’s progress

The report was peppered with caveats. METR said it could be overstating its findings, because the acceleration might only be limited to “well-specified tasks” that can be graded automatically or with a language model, instead of “messy” tasks that are harder to define. Or it could be that Anthropic understated its previous progress, making the latest number look bigger.

METR said it was able to “confidently” rule out the growth of computing power used in training AI models as the reason for the acceleration. Traditionally, the amount of computing power, known as compute, is directly related to how well an AI model performs. The researchers said their guess was that the improvement was down to using AI itself to improve AI.

A key concern, METR said, is that using AI to improve itself could start to compound the acceleration, which could be especially worrying given that researchers found there were no “bottlenecks” such as restrictions on computing power or data holding back Anthropic’s AI progress.

“We understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process,” the report said. However, Anthropic researchers described significant “signs of life” implying that could happen soon, METR said.

Amodei touched on this issue in his September essay, saying AI advances have been driven primarily by the concept of recursive self-improvement, or what he defined as “AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”

“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.

In that same essay, Amodei championed the idea of having external evaluators embedded within the leading AI labs and specifically highlighted METR as an appropriate third-party evaluator. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at the time that he also supported the idea of independent evaluators with employee-like access.

—Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

#10615. Testing JSON-LD Like an API: 7 Checks Before Your Next Release

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A content editor changes an article’s headline. The page updates immediately, but its JSON-LD still contains the previous title. A redesign introduces a new author component while an old plugin continues publishing a different author name in the page source.

Neither failure necessarily produces a JavaScript error. Both leave machines and readers with conflicting descriptions of the same page.

For developers, the useful approach is to treat JSON-LD as a maintained output of the application, with a data source, validation rules, and regression tests. This guide uses a blog template to show how. You will need basic JavaScript knowledge and a modern Node.js installation for the runnable tests.

Requests for search improvements often arrive as broad outcomes: improve discoverability, clarify entities, or support answer engines. These need to become implementation requirements before development starts.

For example, AEO directory includes structured data within descriptions of broader optimization services. For an engineering team, the actionable deliverable is a page representation whose types, properties, and values can be checked against the published content. I personally used this , and adding this because this can help other developer's and designer for optimization and get higher search result's.

For a blog template, define these acceptance criteria:

Keep implementation success separate from search outcomes. Google’s AI features guidance says there is no special Schema.org markup required for its AI search features. Correct markup also does not guarantee rich results or inclusion in an AI-generated answer.

Avoid separate, manually maintained copies of the headline, author, and publication date. Both the visible template and metadata builder should consume the same published record.

Save the following as article-schema.mjs. The builder assumes an upstream content-validation step has already checked required strings, timestamps, and approved HTTPS URLs.

This is a deliberately small example, not a complete rich-result eligibility checklist. Add relevant images and other supported properties when the real page supplies them. Consult the Schema.org BlogPosting definition and Google’s Article documentation for their respective vocabularies and search guidance.

Use a consistent canonical-URL policy before building the identifier: normalize the intended hostname, trailing-slash convention, and query parameters. Do not generate a fresh UUID for the same article on every request.

SitePoint’s guide to implementing JSON-LD on modern websites covers embedding approaches across common stacks.

Valid JSON is not automatically safe to insert into a raw HTML script element.

A CMS value containing can terminate the element at the HTML-parser level, even when the value belongs to a JSON string. Concatenating a headline directly into a script tag is particularly risky.

Append this helper to article-schema.mjs:

JSON serialization handles quotes and backslashes. Replacing literal less-than characters prevents an embedded closing-script sequence from appearing in the resulting text. The Next.js JSON-LD guide documents this approach for script embedding.

Use the serialized result as the content of a script element with type="application/ld+json". Follow your framework’s documented embedding mechanism so the JSON is neither double-encoded nor inserted through an unrelated HTML context.

This helper is specific to JSON-LD script content. It is not a general-purpose HTML sanitizer, URL validator, or substitute for validating CMS data.

The tests should catch changes that would make metadata misleading or unsafe, not merely confirm that an object exists.

Save this file as article-schema.test.mjs beside the builder:

These are unit tests for the builder and serializer. They do not prove that a template embeds the script correctly or that the deployed page is eligible for a search feature. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing helps distinguish those responsibilities.

A passing builder test cannot detect a page component reading a different CMS field.

Add a browser-level check against a controlled article fixture. Inspect its visible heading, byline, dates, canonical link, and JSON-LD together. For this template, assert that the intended article entity appears once and matches those visible fields.

Do not assert that the entire page contains exactly one JSON-LD script. A site may legitimately publish organization, breadcrumb, and article entities separately. Instead, identify the relevant entity by its @id and detect conflicting definitions.

Include these failure cases in the test plan:

Prefer generating metadata from the content loaded during server rendering or static generation when that fits the application. If it is injected client-side, inspect the rendered result and test navigation explicitly. Avoid making essential metadata depend on a user interaction.

No single tool establishes syntax, semantic accuracy, search eligibility, and content consistency at once.

Test both representative code samples and deployed URLs. A validator cannot confirm the truth of an author name simply because the property is syntactically valid.

Google’s general structured-data guidelines also require markup to represent the page accurately. Treat validation warnings as findings to investigate; do not add invented reviews, dates, or attributes merely to improve a tool’s output.

Ownership matters after the first release. Decide which application layer generates article markup, who maintains its mapping, and which publishing events invalidate cached output.

When an editor changes a headline, the visible page and JSON-LD should be rebuilt or refreshed together. Updating one while serving the other from an older cache creates a mismatch even if both implementations are individually correct.

Avoid setting dateModified to the current time on every deployment. A CSS update or infrastructure rebuild does not necessarily mean the article changed. Read the timestamp from the editorial record instead.

Before shipping a template change, run the builder tests, inspect one rendered page per affected template, and check representative deployed URLs. Keep a small fixture set that includes optional fields, long text, translated content, and script-like strings.

A reliable JSON-LD implementation has a traceable relationship with published content. When someone changes the page, its machine-readable description should change predictably—and the test suite should expose the cases where it does not.

AI boom drives record quarterly revenue, but client and gaming business faces double-digit declines going into 2027

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.

As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.

AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.

The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.

AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.

"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.

Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.

Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.

"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."

AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.

As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.

AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.

"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."

For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.

In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.

If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.

The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

#10613. Congress is getting a lot younger: Gen Z members will triple. Here’s the breakdown as midterm election results roll in

The Democrats’ playbook for the midterm elections was to cast a wide net, recruiting candidates that didn’t necessarily look and sound like traditional politicians—and oftentimes, Gen Zers and millennials were part of that.

The results? A historic election that will usher in a wave of 97 Gen Z and millennial leaders into Congress, including 90 members in the House of Representatives, five members in the Senate, and two delegates, according to Future Caucus, the nation’s largest bipartisan organization for Gen Z and millennial lawmakers. Another 15 races are still uncalled, with one headed to a runoff.

Add that up, and the 120th Congress will have at least triple the number of Gen Z members come January, compared with the previous legislature.

Among the new members of the House is 27-year-old Michael Alfonso, the youngest Republican elected to the body. The Cuban American will represent Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. In his acceptance speech, Alfonso said it’s time for younger Americans to have a seat at the table regarding national political issues.

In her first run for office, 29-year-old Democratic Socialist Melat Kiros won in Colorado’s 1st Congressional District, on a platform that addressed young voter issues such as the high cost of living, affordable housing, and universal healthcare. Her message: It’s time to take the power back.

In the Senate, millennials were the generation with the largest number of candidates running in the midterms, with five wins so far.

In May 2025, Democrats held a secret retreat with donors and party officials to expand the Senate map, where Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) encouraged a number of candidates to run, including a young state legislator from Texas named James Talarico, according to reporting by The New York Times.

A year and a half later, 37-year-old Talarico is among the freshman class of millennials about to enter the Senate. This incoming group includes 42-year old Democrat Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, the first Muslim elected to the Senate; 45-year-old Democrat Annie Andrews of South Carolina, a pediatrician and the first woman elected to the body from South Carolina; and 45-year-old Republican Julia Letlow of Louisiana.

As of this writing, 43-year-old Democrat Scott Colom’s run for Mississippi’s seat is too close to call. But if he wins, he would be the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era.

In total, 272 Gen Z and millennial candidates ran in the midterms, winning some 38% of their races that have been called so far, per Future Caucus.

#10609. Can we talk about climate change again? How the blue wave could spark a new era for green policies

“Climate change” wasn’t exactly a prominent topic across 2026 midterm campaigns. But post-election, it’s clear that the climate still won big, and that means more climate action could be right around the corner.

Donald Trump spent the first two years of his second term as president heavily attacking the environment, and the country’s climate efforts. And yet opposing candidates were warned not to focus on the topic.

Addressing “climate change” was “not a priority” for battleground voters, the SearchLight Institute, a think tank founded by Democratic strategist Adam Jantleson, warned last September. 

Many listened to that advice: Out of all Democratic and Republican candidates in eight of the key states in the fight for Senate control (Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, North Caroline, Ohio, Texas), only two mentioned “climate” on their campaign websites, the Guardian reported.

The two candidates, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, both won their bids for the Senate.

Even elected Democrats have embraced “climate hushing” recently. An Inside Climate News analysis of press releases issued by members of the House and Senate found that mentions of climate change plummeted since 2025. 

Climate was (quietly) on the ballot

Still, climate change did appear in the midterms in tangential ways. Candidates railed against AI data centers and soaring energy bills, and many made connections between clean energy investment and lower utility costs. 

And some candidates did outright embrace it. In Michigan, Democrat Will Lawrence, co-creator of the Sunrise Movement—a youth-led advocacy group that helped shape Joe Biden’s climate policies—beat an incumbent Republican, flipping a House seat. 

The incoming Congress, then, is primed to take climate action. It’s a moment that mirrors 2018, when, out of the midterms during Trump’s first term, the Green New Deal emerged, says University of California, Santa Barbara climate and energy policy professor Leah Stokes.

Though critics attacked the Green New Deal, it garnered large public support, and ultimately influenced, and paved the way for, Biden’s landmark climate bill, the Inflation Reduction Act.

“There’s no reason to believe that we couldn’t see the activist energy around data centers transform into being about good-paying, clean energy jobs,” she says. “That vision of a Green New Deal that emerges in the 2018 midterms—it’s very similar to what we could see happening in the coming months.”

Affordable electricity bills are essential to climate solutions.

“If we don’t have cheap, clean electricity, we do not solve the climate crisis,” Stokes says. 

So by addressing high energy costs and the impact of data centers, Congress will help make space for technology like heat pumps and electric vehicles that rely on that cheaper power. 

And as for climate policies, clean energy tax credits could be an easy, quick win that also addresses affordability. 

“The tax credits that Trump rolled back last summer, I think we could see them roll right back forward under the next Congress,” Stokes says.

It’s not unheard of for Republican presidents to push clean energy tax credits, particularly when oil prices are so high. In 1992, for example, Congress passed tax credits for wind energy under George H.W. Bush. In 2005, under George W. Bush, solar energy tax credits passed. 

Despite the environmental destruction that Trump has unleashed so far, Stokes is hopeful about how things could switch after these midterm results. “Things can change quickly,” she says.

#10605. The midterms weren’t the rebuke of AI money many expected

The midterms are shaping up to be a record-breaking election for Democrats, who have flipped states including South Carolina and Texas. But the election has also shattered records for private political spending. By some estimates, super PAC spending exceeded $2 billion this cycle, more than 50% above previous election cycles.

One of the dominant narratives heading into the midterms was that Big Tech—and the artificial intelligence sector in particular—would spend hundreds of millions of dollars electing AI-friendly lawmakers, much as the cryptocurrency industry had done in previous elections. Indeed, Leading the Future, the largest pro-AI super PAC network, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Greg Brockman, and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, invited comparisons to the crypto super PAC network Fairshake, drawing on some of the same donors and political operatives. (Both networks operate through partisan affiliates: Leading the Future has Think Big for Democrats and American Mission for Republicans, while Fairshake’s got Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, respectively.)

But as public sentiment toward AI soured and Democratic Party insiders warned candidates against accepting industry money, the narrative began to shift. Yet a Fast Company analysis of election data suggests the midterms were hardly the rebuke of AI money that some had anticipated. More than 86% of the candidates backed by Leading the Future have won or are currently leading their House or Senate races. That’s roughly on par with Fairshake, which supported 87 candidates this cycle, 77 of whom have won or are currently ahead.

The two industries’ political efforts also appear to be converging. Leading the Future and Fairshake backed 21 of the same candidates, including Rep. Kevin Hern, who won his Senate race in Oklahoma. Hern also received support from the Anthropic-funded Public First, which has positioned itself as a counterweight to the industry’s other political spending operations.

Big Crypto outspent the AI industry but achieved similar results

While Big Crypto outspent the largest AI industry super PACs this election cycle and backed more candidates, the groups saw broadly similar results. Fairshake, the cryptocurrency super PAC funded by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, spent about $154 million this cycle, compared with $34.8 million by Leading the Future and $24.4 million by Public First. Yet roughly comparable shares of the candidates each group supported won their elections.

Of the 12 Senate candidates backed by Leading the Future, nine won their races, compared with five of Fairshake’s eight candidates. Both Senate candidates supported by Public First—Kevin Hern in Oklahoma and Pete Ricketts in Nebraska—also won. In the House, Leading the Future’s candidates won 31 of 38 races, compared with six of 11 for Public First and 63 of 79 for Fairshake.

Analysts had previously noted that Leading the Future appeared to be playing it safe, largely backing incumbents. But Fast Company’s analysis found that just over half of its 40 winning candidates were incumbents. The group also spent considerably more, on average, backing non-incumbents: roughly $511,000 per candidate, compared with $288,100 for incumbents.

Several of Leading the Future’s biggest investments paid off. Among its winning candidates were Louisiana Republican Julia Letlow, whom the group backed with $1.17 million; Utah Democrat Ben McAdams, who received $1.12 million in support; and New York Democrat Ritchie Torres, who received $1.16 million.

But heavy spending was no guarantee of success. Two of the 10 candidates on whom Leading the Future spent the most lost their races.

Arguably the AI industry’s biggest setback came in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Leading the Future spent about $2.3 million supporting Graham—more than it spent on any other candidate. Another pro-AI super PAC, Building the Future, poured an additional $2.5 million into the race, the only contest it has reported spending on. Yet Andrews, a former pediatrician, pulled off a historic victory in the Republican stronghold without financial backing from either AI or crypto super PACs.

Leading the Future also spent nearly $1.4 million on Jesse Jackson Jr., the disgraced former Illinois congressman who resigned amid a federal corruption investigation. He didn’t make it past his primary.

Public First suffered several high-profile defeats of its own. The group spent roughly $13 million backing New York Democrat Alex Bores, who lost his primary. Other losing candidates who received substantial support included Texas Republican Carlos De La Cruz Jr. ($1.5 million), Alabama Republican Rhett Marques ($960,000), and Texas Republican Alexandra Mealer ($905,000).

Fairshake likewise saw some of its biggest bets fail. The group spent $36.8 million supporting Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and another $19.7 million opposing his Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown. Brown won. Fairshake’s second-largest investment, however, paid off: Alabama Republican Barry Moore won his Senate race after receiving $12.2 million in support.

The group also spent millions trying unsuccessfully to defeat several Democrats, including Illinois Senate candidate Juliana Stratton, whom it spent nearly $10 million opposing. Three House Democrats also prevailed despite Fairshake’s opposition: La Shawn Ford in Illinois ($2.5 million), Oliver Gilbert in Florida ($2.1 million), and Donavan McKinney in Michigan ($269,000).

AI Super PAC spending peaked during the primaries, then cooled heading into the general election

Weekly spending by the largest AI super PACs surged in June, coinciding with the closely watched Democratic primary of Alex Bores in New York. Bores, a New York Assembly member and former Palantir data scientist turned AI safety advocate, lost after Leading the Future poured $8 million into opposing his candidacy. The Anthropic-backed Public First, meanwhile, spent roughly $10 million of its $13 million investment in Bores that same month.

Bores lost to fellow Assembly member Micah Lasher, who went on to appear on the general-election ballot in New York’s 12th Congressional District. Neither super PAC spent money supporting or opposing Lasher.

But AI money, especially toward the end of the election cycle, was dwarfed by Big Crypto.

In October, Fairshake spent $57.6 million, largely on advertising and media buys, compared with $4.1 million by Leading the Future and just over $1 million by Public First.

Industry observers have attributed that disparity, at least in part, to AI’s growing unpopularity across the political spectrum. A September Pew Research Center poll found that 56% of Democrats were concerned about the impact of AI, compared with 46% of Republicans—a relatively narrow partisan divide in an otherwise polarized political climate.

Even so, both Leading the Future and Public First backed more Republicans than Democrats. Leading the Future supported 34 Republicans and 16 Democrats, spending money to oppose just one candidate: Bores. Of the Republicans it backed, 28 won or are currently leading their races, compared with 15 of the 16 Democrats. Public First supported eight Republicans and five Democrats, while spending $1.4 million opposing three Republicans. Four of its five Democratic candidates won, compared with four of its eight Republicans.

Despite the prevailing view that Democrats see AI money as toxic, Big AI has still spent an outsized amount supporting Democratic candidates. On average, Leading the Future spent nearly twice as much per Democratic candidate than Republican. 

Public First’s spending followed a somewhat different pattern. Although it spent more overall supporting Democrats, largely because of its $13 million investment in Bores, its median spending per Republican candidate was higher.

That spending came despite a public backlash from within the Democratic Party. More than 100 Democratic operatives signed an open letter urging candidates to reject money from AI companies. Yet the industry’s political spending continued, often with little mention of AI itself. As NBC News reported, ads funded by AI groups rarely highlighted candidates’ positions on the technology.

There is also a convergence between the candidates Big Crypto and Big AI support. Leading the Future and Fairshake backed 20 of the same candidates this cycle, including New York Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres, who received $1.4 million in support from Fairshake and $1.1 million from Leading the Future. Alabama Republican Barry Moore also benefited from both groups, receiving $12.2 million in support from Fairshake and roughly $330,000 from Leading the Future.

As public sentiment sours, the industry faces a wave of potential legislative and regulatory challenges. Democratic gains in Congress could mean greater scrutiny of AI companies, which have until now enjoyed powerful allies in the House, Senate, and White House. Proposals ranging from state and federal data center moratoriums to restrictions on the development of artificial superintelligence could help shape the industry’s future.

When the new Congress convenes, roughly one in 13 House members and a quarter of newly elected senators will have benefited from Leading the Future’s support. For a super PAC that didn’t exist two years ago, that’s a remarkable foothold. Whether it translates into political power is another question.

Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.”

In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks of severance or more, depending on their tenure, equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare, any corporate devices, and an extra $5,000. 

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

#10600. Scientists are rethinking what menopause does to the brain. Here’s what they discovered

Hormones change as we age in dramatic ways that can alter our mental and physical health – and the science around those hormones is changing too.

A new study just published in the journal Neurology sheds new light on the ways that estrogen may protect the brain as it ages, and the results are promising.

The research examined the health outcomes among 352 cognitively unimpaired women who underwent a brain MRI at age 70 and again five years after the first scan. Out of the group, women who had longer lifetime exposure to estrogen through oral birth control and menopausal hormone therapy showed fewer physiological markers associated with Alzheimer’s and had healthier brains overall.

Scientists have already established a connection between longer reproductive spans – basically, the number of years after periods start and before they stop – with reduced brain aging later in life. That research and other findings suggest that estrogen has a strong neuroprotective effect, basically working as armor for the brain against cognitive decline. But as women and other people with periods age, their estrogen levels begin to decline, lowering the hormonal barrier that protects the brain during the body’s reproductive years.

Giving the brain a boost

Estrogen supports cognitive health in a number of ways. Those functions include reducing inflammation, boosting blood flow, and protecting the brain’s white matter – the connective tissue that works as a superhighway between neurons.

“The long-term impact of endogenous and exogenous estrogen fluctuations on late-life [cerebral small vessel disease] severity remains poorly understood,” the paper’s authors wrote. That condition is associated with cognitive deterioration and Alzheimer’s, a devastating disease that is almost twice as common in women compared to men.

“Previous studies have linked longer reproductive span, earlier [periods], and later menopause to reduced brain aging, reinforcing the neuroprotective role of estradiol,” the authors wrote. “…While longer lifetime estrogen exposure may provide neuroprotection, abrupt estrogen loss may increase neuropathology accumulation and dementia risk.”

The new research is important because it shows a link between external or “exogenous” sources of estrogen and improved brain health. While doctors can’t dictate how long a person’s brain might be protected by naturally-occurring endogenous estrogen, exogenous estrogen is readily available through birth control pills, hormonal patches, and topical creams.

A changing story about estrogen

The conversation around estrogen has been in the midst of a seismic shift.

A year ago, the FDA removed black box warning labels from hormone-based drugs used to treat perimenopause and menopause symptoms. The serious safety warning was first put in place more than two decades ago and cautioned doctors that estrogen-based drugs could raise the risk of heart issues and blood clots. For years, the black box warning scared many patients and doctors away from supplementary estrogen, in spite of research that showed that estrogen-based drugs were safe for many people.

Since the black box warning was lifted, estrogen is undergoing something of a renaissance. More people are talking openly about what they experience during menopause and perimenopause, the hormonally chaotic phase before the body fully moves into menopause. For many women, those hormonal changes crash into their personal and professional lives with an array of mood and physical symptoms that go well beyond hot flashes. The changing discourse has been a boon for telehealth providers like Midi as a whole generation of women explore the fact that a simple patch, pill, or gel might boost their quality of life considerably.

“With few exceptions, there may be no other medication in the modern era that can improve the health outcomes of women at a population level more than hormone replacement therapy,” former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary said last year, extolling the long term benefits of hormone therapy as “tremendous.”

The tremendous promise of relief for symptoms like brain fog, hot flashes, depression, and anxiety has been enough to drive a nationwide shortage of estrogen patches. As new research delves deeper into the ways that estrogen may protect the aging brain, many women will have one more reason to hit up their doctor for a chat about hormone therapy. —-

AI-powered software cloning is quite the hot topic. Software companies are likely unhappy with the notion of vibe coders ganging up to try and copy their software. Simultaneously, users tired of subscription models, price hikes, and drops in software quality are more than happy to rebel, as proven by the buzz around the Adobe-replacement ArtCraft. Now, OccupySaaS is the latest user-led revolt against the software system, aiming to create clean-room, open-source reimplementations of common services using AI tools.

The initiatives already underway in the project look to replace Auth0 and Salesforce with minty fresh alternatives called ZeroAuthy and SalesCompel, respectively. Given that these services all run on their companies' servers, there are no binaries to examine and decompile — the reimplementations are done referencing available documentation, APIs, development kit behaviors, and any applicable open standards. Judging from the project website, it seemingly wants new software to acts as a API-compatible drop-in replacement where applicable.

The project puts a sharp pin on its development ethics and requirements: all work must be a fully clean-room reimplementation, with no decompiled code, no confidential information (including source code) taken from any previous employers, and no copying of UI assets or any other trademarks.

Creating software in this manner is both easier and harder than usual. On the one hand, the only thing that matters is that whichever user inputs are processed and produce the same outputs as the original software, and those behaviors are largely defined by the aforementioned specifications.

At the same time, hosted software is effectively a black box with internal behaviors and "gotchas" that aren't immediately obvious. Just as with console emulators, any drop-in replacement needs to reproduce extant API bugs to be fully compatible — looking at you, Jira.

Besides the aforementioned services, OccupySaaS intends to find replacements for services offering document-and-wiki management, issue tracking, software feature flagging, software/server observability, and customer support. Our guesses for the targeted replacements in each of those categories are Confluence, Jira, LaunchDarkly, Datadog, and Zendesk.

The language of choice is Go, picked over Rust simply because it allows for easily compiling and linking all its dependencies into the one binary that doesn't need an installer and can just be copied to a target system and executed. According to OccupySaaS, that characteristic makes it ideal for packaging into a Docker container or other forms of self-hosting.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Some people may quickly point out that the entire point of renting a SaaS to begin with is that any snafu with the code or the infrastructure is always Someone Else's Problem, and that running your own instance is backwards. However, since OccupySaaS's software is Apache 2.0-licensed, there's nothing stopping anyone from providing a service for it. Examples include Red Hat Enterprise Linux, GitLab, and of course, Wordpress.

The project appears to be the brainchild of Thomas Meadows, a software engineer with two decades of experience. In his personal homepage, he claims is strong suit is project management, which is a good skill to have in this day and age of directing AI agents towards a goal. The website reads like a manifesto, pointing out that per-seat licensing taxes growth, and that the same people who created the software are now being fired — "the software built by the 99% belongs to the 99%."

#10596. Apple is slashing AI budgets—the latest company to do so

Tokenmaxxing is on the way out, even as some of the biggest players in the tech industry are urging their employees to use AI as much as possible. A new Bloomberg report reveals that Apple is cutting employee budgets for AI token usage while remaining just as committed to deploying AI to boost efficiency. 

Apple has already reduced the daily spending limit from $300 to $200 for certain engineers, according to Bloomberg, but the company reportedly plans to cut that down even more. Sources told Bloomberg that the daily cap could drop as low as $100 for some engineering teams. In many other departments, daily AI spending is already capped at $100; now Apple is considering reducing the limit to $25 for certain teams. 

The spending limit is measured in tokens, which are units of AI usage that represent fragments of text or data processed by AI systems. 

This move comes as Apple continues pressing its engineers and other employees to use AI more in day to day operations. But it also reflects a larger trend rippling across the tech industry, as companies struggle to justify their outsized spending on AI. 

After pushing their employees to adopt AI, many tech employers seem to be grappling with the fact that those investments have not yielded the productivity gains that they anticipated. 

According to Bloomberg, some Apple employees believed many people weren’t making use of the $300 limit and that it was higher than needed. But other employees seemed to view it as a sign that Apple is looking to reduce costs—and that the company could resort to layoffs. 

Bloomberg reports that Apple is already taking steps to streamline their operations in the interest of maximizing efficiency, and recently-appointed CEO John Ternus is reportedly already advocating for reducing layers of management (something that Amazon has also sought to do over the last year).

There are plenty of signs tech companies are tightening their belts, even as they continue to prioritize AI adoption across their workforce. Uber exhausted its annual AI budget in a matter of months, leading the company to cap monthly spending at $1,500 for each AI coding tool. Companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla have all imposed token limits on their employees. 

Beyond AI spend, however, the fear of layoffs looms large across the tech industry. 

A steady stream of employers have trimmed headcount in the last year due to AI investments, either to offset exorbitant AI spending, or because AI has enabled them to cut back on certain jobs. A number of companies, including Microsoft, have given their workers the option of taking a voluntary buyout, presumably to stave off job losses or avoid the negative attention associated with major layoffs. 

As Fast Company reported this week, some workers have even started to worry about AI being used to select employees for layoffs as companies shed jobs and reshape their workforce. In other words, it seems companies are continuing to demand more of their employees, but with less support—human or otherwise.

#10595. Google shuts down a sneaky malware backdoor on millions of Android TV and Google TV boxes

Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole.

In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with “Videostrong,” a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes. This is due to the company building in a backdoor that it could sell access to, including the distribution of malware. Google has taken legal action to block the domains and servers that “Videostrong” was using to control the XCPE botnet and malware modules and banned the company and its subsidiaries from selling certified Android devices going forward, or selling software to any other certified vendors.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Synthient (via The Hacker News) compiled a list of potentially affected devices, with the focus being on the Mecool brand that has made some well-known Android TV and Google TV boxes in the past. Mecool has been rumored to be shutting down.

Google somewhat admits that this was a failing on its part, as these devices were sold as “certified” Android devices with the implication that they were safe. The company explains that these bad actors “employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot.” With that in mind, Google is updating its review process to protect users against this type of behavior, and Google reiterates that “a device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust.”

Google’s shutdown of the domains and servers used to spread malware should leave affected Android TV and Google TV boxes safe to use – the company says that “taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices” – but owners may still want to consider alternate options.

Learning to code can feel overwhelming at first. There are different programming languages, development tools, and concepts to understand, and choosing where to begin is not always easy. Coding apps can make the process more approachable by breaking lessons into smaller steps and giving beginners a place to practice what they learn.

Whether you want to build websites, develop software, or explore programming as a new skill, the right app can help you get started. Some platforms focus on interactive lessons, while others offer coding exercises, guided projects, or access to a full development environment.

Here are six coding apps worth considering if you're learning programming for the first time.

Mimo is a beginner-friendly coding app designed to help users learn programming through short lessons and interactive exercises. Rather than starting with lengthy explanations, it introduces concepts in manageable steps, making it easier to fit learning into a busy schedule.

The app covers several topics, including Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SQL. This makes it useful for beginners who want to explore general programming or focus on web development. As learners progress, they can work through structured learning paths and practice applying concepts through coding exercises and projects.

Mimo is particularly suitable for people who prefer a guided learning experience instead of figuring out what to study next on their own. Its mobile-first approach also makes it convenient to practice during breaks or while traveling.

A free starting option is available, although access to some courses and features requires a paid plan.

Best for: Beginners who want structured lessons and practical coding exercises.

SoloLearn is a coding education platform that helps beginners explore programming languages through short lessons, quizzes, and hands-on practice. It is a useful starting point for people who want to understand programming fundamentals before committing to a specific development path.

The platform offers courses in languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, SQL, HTML, and CSS. Its bite-sized lessons make complicated topics easier to approach, while interactive exercises let learners test their understanding as they progress.

Another useful feature is its learning community, where users can explore other people's code, participate in discussions, and learn from different approaches to programming problems.

SoloLearn works well for people who are still deciding which language to learn. However, completing lessons alone is not enough to develop strong programming skills. Beginners should also practice writing their own programs and building small projects.

The platform offers free learning options alongside paid features.

Best for: Beginners who want to explore multiple programming languages and learn through short, interactive lessons.

Codecademy Go is the mobile companion to Codecademy's online learning platform. It is designed to help learners reinforce programming concepts and review material while away from their computers.

Codecademy's broader learning platform offers courses covering web development, Python, JavaScript, SQL, and other technical subjects. The mobile app can be useful for reviewing concepts, practicing through supported activities, and maintaining a consistent learning routine between longer study sessions.

For example, someone taking a JavaScript course on a computer can use the mobile experience to revisit concepts and strengthen their understanding before returning to practical exercises.

It is important to distinguish between learning on a mobile device and developing software on one. Codecademy Go is primarily a companion for learning and review rather than a complete replacement for a desktop coding environment.

Some learning content is available without a subscription, while access to additional courses and features depends on the current plan.

Best for: Learners who want to review programming concepts alongside a structured online course.

Programming Hub is an educational app for people who want to explore programming and related technical subjects in one place. It brings together lessons, examples, and exercises designed to introduce users to different areas of software development.

Its learning material covers languages such as Python, Java, C++, and JavaScript, along with web development and other computing topics. This variety can be helpful for beginners who want to compare different languages before choosing one to study in depth.

The app's lesson-based approach makes it possible to explore a topic without immediately installing a development environment or configuring complicated software. Code examples and practice activities can also help learners connect theoretical concepts with practical applications.

However, beginners should avoid jumping between too many languages at once. Starting with one language, understanding its fundamentals, and applying those skills to a small project will generally provide a stronger foundation.

Programming Hub offers free and paid options, with access depending on the selected plan.

Best for: Beginners who want an introduction to several programming languages and computing topics.

Enki takes a slightly different approach to learning programming by emphasizing regular practice and the development of technical skills over time. Its lessons and exercises are designed to help users strengthen their understanding through consistent, manageable learning sessions.

Depending on the learning content available, users can explore topics such as Python, SQL, JavaScript, data analysis, and other areas of technology. This makes the app relevant to both aspiring developers and people who want to improve their technical knowledge for work.

One advantage of short, recurring practice sessions is that they encourage learners to revisit concepts instead of studying them once and moving on. Regular revision can help reinforce programming syntax, terminology, and problem-solving techniques.

Enki may be especially useful for people who already have some exposure to coding and want to maintain a learning habit. Complete beginners should check whether the available lessons match their chosen language and current skill level before starting.

The app offers different access options, so check its current listing for details about free and paid features.

Best for: Learners who prefer regular practice and gradual improvement in technical skills.

Replit is a browser-based development platform that allows users to write, run, and test code without setting up a traditional development environment on their computer. It is particularly useful for beginners who want to move beyond lessons and start creating their own programs.

Users can work with languages and technologies such as Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, depending on the project and environment. Instead of only answering quiz questions, learners can experiment with code, identify errors, and see how their changes affect a working application.

For example, a beginner learning Python could create a simple calculator, while someone studying web development could build a basic personal website. Starting with small projects helps learners understand how individual programming concepts work together.

Replit also provides AI-assisted development features, which can help users explore ideas and understand code. However, beginners should review generated code and learn why it works rather than relying on automated suggestions without understanding them.

Replit offers a free starting option, with additional capabilities available through paid plans. Features and usage limits may vary.

Best for: Beginners who want to practice writing code and experiment with real projects in a development environment.

The best coding app depends on your learning goals, preferred learning style, and current experience. Before choosing one, consider what you want to accomplish.

Choose a language first. If you want to learn general programming, Python is a reasonable starting point. If your goal is to build websites, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are more directly relevant.

Consider how you learn. Apps such as Mimo and SoloLearn emphasize short lessons and interactive practice. Codecademy Go is useful for reviewing course material, while Replit provides an environment for experimenting with code.

Look for practical exercises. Understanding a lesson is only the beginning. Choose resources that encourage you to write code, solve problems, and apply concepts in small projects.

Check the cost. Several coding apps provide free introductory content, but some courses and advanced features may require subscriptions. Review the current pricing before committing to a paid plan.

Move beyond the app. As your skills improve, practice using a computer, read technical documentation, and create projects of your own. These activities help you develop the problem-solving skills required for real programming work.

Coding apps provide an accessible way to begin learning programming without needing extensive technical knowledge or complicated software installations. They can help you understand basic concepts, practice regularly, and discover which areas of development interest you most.

Mimo and SoloLearn are worth exploring if you prefer guided lessons, while Codecademy Go can complement a structured course. Programming Hub and Enki offer alternative approaches to learning and practice, and Replit provides a way to experiment with working code.

You do not need to master every programming language or use several apps simultaneously. Start with one resource, focus on a single learning goal, and gradually apply what you learn to practical projects. Consistent practice and curiosity will take you further than simply completing lessons.

#10592. The Meta Quest 2 and Quest Pro are receiving their last OS updates soon. Here’s what you need to know

The best-selling VR headset of all time (and its Pro-level cousin) will no longer receive OS updates after March 2027.

Somehow, the Meta Quest 2 has been around for six whopping years, and Meta is finally bringing support for the headset to a close after March 2027. The far less popular Meta Quest Pro, which uses the same chipset as the Quest 2, will also see OS updates cease at the same time with OS v213. Meta will continue to deliver security updates through the end of 2027 to both headsets, according to an official Meta developers blog post.

Meta says it will not be removing cross-play multiplayer functionality or blocking access to Quest 2 players, so any games that support the headset will continue to work after these dates, so long as they don’t rely on any new OS features introduced after March 2027. Developers have to give players a 6-month notice if support is ending for a game, so you’ll have ample time to decide what to do.

That means the Quest 2 will receive just over 7 years of total security updates, while the Quest Pro gets two years less (since it came out in October 2022). The Meta Quest 2 remains the best-selling VR headset of all time, with around 20 million units sold over the lifetime of the headset. Meta says that Quest 2 owners can still play games throughout this time, although game support will likely dry up quickly after January 2028.

The $599 Meta Quest 3 and $349 Meta Quest 3S, which debuted in 2023 and 2024, respectively, are the follow-ups to the Quest 2. The upcoming Meta VR Glasses, which will retail for $1299, feature a next-generation chipset, a significantly higher-resolution AMOLED display, and substantially lighter weight and smaller size than either Quest 3 model.

Meta VR Glasses are expected to debut early next year, and with them, a new generation of OS development will take place. Since the Quest 2 uses a significantly outdated mobile chip at this point, it makes sense for Meta to cease new feature development for it and focus on newer, more capable hardware.

Developer is aiming for 30 Hz performance on Intel Panther Lake NPUs but the current version of this research driver is only achieving 2 to 3 Hz.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A developer group by the name of labscommunity has released a prototype driver for Windows 11 that renders the desktop using an NPU instead of the system’s (i)GPU. The new driver is called npu-driver, and the open-source (Apache 2.0) code is available on GitHub. It has been tested on Intel Panther Lake systems, and while it isn’t hitting its 30 Hz performance target yet, it is clever enough to fall back to GPU on request or on any fault.

The reasoning behind the development of this driver may strike a chord with those observing the 2020s processor landscape. “Every new laptop ships an NPU that sits idle while the GPU composes the desktop, runs the browser and, increasingly, runs local models,” notes the npu-driver readme file. “The question this project asks is narrow and testable: can the NPU take over desktop composition, end-to-end, without the applications or the compositor knowing?”

Thankfully, the answer to the question about whether the NPU can render the Windows 11 desktop - and apps like Notepad and Edge windows - is a yes. The npu-driver functions as intended and as demonstrated. Moreover, it seamlessly switches back to GPU rendering if/when it needs to.

The developer admits that this driver is strictly “a research prototype, not a product” at this stage, and the main issue currently is performance. The GitHub readme notes that the target 30 Hz performance isn’t very close right now, with actual screen refresh speeds of around 2 to 3 Hz. npu-driver is being developed on a Panther Lake laptop, and all these Intel processors feature NPU 5 architecture silicon with performance spanning 45-50 TOPS.

A Reddit post that appears to be penned by one of the labscommunity crew says that this project might render Windows 11 visuals rather slowly, but it can “bring 3D GPU usage down from 3.4% to 0.6%,” thus freeing up the GPU for other tasks, like inference.

Having a(nother) useful task for the system NPU to do is a welcome development, even if it seems of rather niche appeal for now. There are no signs consumer processors will abandon NPU integration, and these accelerators will likely remain alongside other now-essentials like hardware for video (de)coding, DSPs, and so on, even if the Copilot+ PC branding exercise has been abandoned by Microsoft and its partners.

An AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

I am not a cheapskate, but I learned quickly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

Along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

Coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features quickly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

My setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

Claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated users ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

The test also showed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

Oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

#10582. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.
